guide.title: About JIF files
guide.markdown:
### What is a JIF file?

JIF is short for JPEG Interchange Format, the first file layout the JPEG standard defined for holding JPEG-compressed pictures. JFIF and Exif largely took its place, and .jif files are rarely seen now. Most files with a JPEG picture inside today use one of those two layouts.

The compression inside is JPEG, a method the Joint Photographic Experts Group started designing in 1986. The core text is ITU-T T.81 from 1992, which ISO and IEC took on as 10918-1 two years later. Baseline JPEG discards detail by design: 8x8 blocks of pixels pass through a discrete cosine transform, and the results are Huffman-coded. Most digital cameras and scanners write JPEG natively. The format itself is free to use now that its US patents have lapsed, and every major browser displays it, so JPEG is rarely the obstacle. That is the usual reason to convert: the picture is fine, the file name is the problem. JIF is also easy to mistake for GIF, a different format with a 256-color palette and optional animation.

A JIF is used for legacy JPEG files and for interchange of JPEG photographs. A JPG is the form of the same compression that cameras, scanners, web pages and photo sharing sites handle every day, and the two endings, .jpg and .jpeg, mean the same thing. The registered media type is image/jpeg. Converting here changes the layout and the name, and the pixels are decoded and compressed again, so the JPG is a new file rather than a renamed copy.

### Programs that open JIF files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** XnView lists JIF among the formats it opens. The JPG made here opens in any web browser, in Preview on macOS, in Windows Photos and in GIMP.

### JIF and JPG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: the original layout uses .jif, while the file most programs expect uses .jpg or .jpeg, with image/jpeg as its media type.
- **Compression**: identical. A discrete cosine transform works on 8x8 pixel blocks, and Huffman coding packs the result.
- **Transparency**: neither has an alpha channel, so a JPEG cannot hold transparency.
- **Color depth**: 8 bits for each color channel.
- **Layers**: JPEG cannot store layers.
- **Layout**: JIF is the layout from the standard itself. JFIF and Exif largely replaced it.
- **Quality scale**: editors usually offer a 0 to 100 slider, and equal numbers do not mean equal quality across programs. GIMP's default is 85. This page asks the canvas encoder for 0.85 on its 0 to 1 scale.
- **Progressive mode**: a progressive JPEG paints a rough version first and refines it as the rest of the file arrives.
- **Acceptance**: a form that wants a JPG often checks the ending, so a .jif name can be turned away even when the data would display.

Here the page asks your browser's image decoder to read the file, then saves a JPG at quality 0.85 and the original pixel dimensions. Since both formats are lossy, this is a second round of compression, and EXIF, ICC and XMP data stay behind.

### Other ways to convert JIF to JPG

- **GIMP (any desktop):** bring the picture in, go to File > Export As, name the output with a .jpg ending and press Export. A JPEG settings dialog follows, where you choose the quality. GIMP's JPEG export defaults to 85 and keeps neither transparency nor layers.
- **Photopea (web):** choose File > Open for the picture, then File > Export As > JPG and save the download.

### Problems with JIF files

- **Your editor will not open it**: Use the converter above and open the JPG in any viewer.
- **A form rejects the file**: convert it here and upload the .jpg instead.
- **"Image decode failed."**: the browser could not read the picture. Download the file again, since a transfer that stopped early leaves a file that ends in the middle.
- **It turns out to be a GIF**: GIF and JIF differ by one letter, and a GIF is a different format. Check the full extension before converting.
- **Quality settings differ**: a quality number in one program does not match the same number in another, so compare results by eye rather than by number.
- **Camera details are gone**: the conversion passes through raw pixels and drops EXIF. Read those details from the JIF before converting.

guide.title: About JPEG files
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPEG file?

Behind the name is the Joint Photographic Experts Group, which started on the format in 1986. The specification dates to 1992 as ITU-T T.81 and was adopted internationally in 1994 as ISO/IEC 10918-1. JPEG was designed for photographs. Baseline coding sends 8x8 pixel blocks through a discrete cosine transform, packs the output with Huffman codes and drops the detail the eye is least likely to notice.

People use JPEG for web photographs, pictures straight off a camera, mail attachments and photo-sharing sites, and most cameras and scanners write it. The US patents lapsed in October 2006, and all major browsers show the format. A progressive mode lets a rough image appear first and clear up as the file loads. You will see both .jpg and .jpeg; they are one format, registered as image/jpeg.

### Programs that open JPEG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** Preview on macOS and Windows Photos show JPEG, GIMP edits it, and ImageMagick converts it from a terminal.
- **Web:** Chrome and Firefox display JPG in a tab.
- **Mobile:** Safari displays JPG on iPhone and iPad.

### JPEG and TIFF compared

- **Extensions**: .jpg and .jpeg (image/jpeg) versus .tif and .tiff (image/tiff).
- **Compression**: baseline JPEG is always lossy. TIFF is a tag-based wrapper: it can use different compression methods, lossless or lossy, and different color representations.
- **Size**: a TIFF made on this page can be much larger than the JPEG it came from.
- **Quality scale**: JPEG sliders run 0 to 100 and GIMP's default is 85. This page has no quality setting for TIFF output.
- **Pages**: a JPEG is one picture. A TIFF can contain several images, which makes it useful for scanned document sequences.
- **Bit depth**: a JPEG has 8 bits for each channel. TIFF is established for high-bit-depth imaging, though a TIFF written from this page is 8-bit.
- **Transparency**: JPEG has no alpha channel.
- **Standing**: Aldus and Microsoft created TIFF, revision 6.0 is from 1992, and Adobe now controls the specification. Preservation master files are an established use.
- **Limits**: the 32-bit offsets in classic TIFF cap a file at roughly 4 GB, a ceiling BigTIFF lifts with wider ones.

In this conversion the browser decodes the JPEG, and ImageMagick running in the page encodes the pixels as a TIFF. The TIFF holds the decoded pixels as they are, so no second JPEG compression is applied. EXIF, ICC profiles and XMP stay behind. The download takes the JPEG's name with a .tiff ending, and the JPEG file itself is not changed.

The TIFF made here holds one image. A TIFF can hold several, so software that exposes the full image sequence is needed to see them all, and software may skip private tags, such as certain color-profile extensions.

### Other ways to convert JPEG to TIFF

- **Preview (Mac):** open the picture, go to File > Export, set Format to TIFF and save.
- **GIMP (any desktop):** pick File > Export As with a .tiff extension, then select a compression in the TIFF dialog, which offers None, LZW, Pack Bits, Deflate, JPEG and CCITT. LZW and Deflate are lossless; JPEG compression inside a TIFF is lossy.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick input.jpeg -compress LZW output.tiff`. LZW is one of ImageMagick's listed compression types, and options go before the output file name.

### Problems with JPEG files

- **Blocky squares or halos**: heavy compression leaves 8x8 block edges. A TIFF made from that file keeps them, so start from the least compressed version you have.
- **Transparency**: a JPEG cannot hold see-through areas, and a TIFF made from one has none to show.
- **Layers are gone**: a JPEG is one flat picture, so the layered project file is the thing to keep.
- **An old photo frame will not show it**: some older devices reject progressive JPEG, and saving it again without progressive mode fixes that.
- **Quality numbers do not match**: the same quality number in two editors can give different file sizes and looks, so judge the result by eye.
- **A job asks for 16-bit**: a JPEG source has only 8 bits per channel and the TIFF here stays 8-bit, so no extra depth appears. Ask for the original capture if the job needs it.
- **"Image decode failed."**: your browser could not read the JPEG. Download the JPEG again and retry.

guide.title: About JPG files
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPG file?

A JPG holds a picture squeezed by the method the Joint Photographic Experts Group began developing in 1986. The standard text exists as ITU-T Recommendation T.81 (1992) and as international standard ISO/IEC 10918-1 (1994). Baseline compression is lossy. Pixels are handled in 8x8 blocks, a discrete cosine transform turns each block into coefficients, and Huffman codes store them.

JPG is everywhere because cameras and scanners write it natively and browsers draw it without help. US patent protection ended in October 2006. Both .jpg and .jpeg name this one format, served as image/jpeg.

### Programs that open JPG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** ImageMagick reads JPG on the command line, and GIMP imports the picture if you want to touch it up first.
- **Web:** Chrome and Firefox draw JPG in a tab.
- **Mobile:** Safari shows JPG on iPhone and iPad.

### JPG and AVIF compared

- **Extensions**: .jpg or .jpeg (image/jpeg) against .avif (image/avif).
- **Compression**: JPEG applies a block-based discrete cosine transform followed by Huffman coding. AVIF packs AV1-compressed images into the HEIF container and offers lossy and lossless modes.
- **Transparency**: JPEG has no alpha channel. AVIF does.
- **Color depth**: 8 bits for each JPEG channel; AVIF goes up to 12 for HDR and wide gamut, though this page writes 8.
- **Quality scale**: editors tend to offer 0 to 100, but a given number does not mean the same quality everywhere. This page has no quality control of its own.
- **Layers**: JPEG cannot store layers.
- **Metadata**: Exif, XMP and an ICC profile all fit in an AVIF file; this page writes none of them.
- **Origins**: the Alliance for Open Media started in 2015 with a goal of royalty-free media formats, and AV1 appeared in 2018.
- **Large pictures**: Baseline-profile AVIF items top out at 8,192 x 4,352 pixels; bigger pictures are tiled as a grid.
- **Licensing**: AVIF is royalty-free.
- **Speed**: AVIF images are slow to decode, and encoding one can take several seconds. JPEG is quick both ways.
- **Progressive display**: a progressive JPG shows a rough picture early, while an AVIF does not render progressively.
- **Support**: every browser shows JPEG. AVIF displays in current Chrome, Firefox, Safari and Edge, and Android decodes it from version 12. Older browsers may not show AVIF, so keep a JPEG, PNG or WebP copy for visitors whose browser cannot open AVIF. Windows needs two Microsoft add-ons to preview .avif files: the HEIF Image Extension plus the AV1 Video Extension.

For the conversion, your browser decodes the JPG into pixels. If the browser's canvas can encode AVIF, the page asks it for the AVIF. If it cannot, it returns a PNG, and an ImageMagick build running inside the page writes the AVIF from that. Either way the picture keeps its pixel size and loses its metadata, and the AVIF has 8 bits per channel. Nothing leaves your device, because both the decoding and the encoding happen in the browser tab and the original JPG is left as it was. The download uses the JPG's name with an .avif ending.

### Other ways to convert JPG to AVIF

- **GIMP (any desktop):** use File > Export As, enter a filename that ends in .avif, press Export and accept the AVIF settings.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick photo.jpg photo.avif`. ImageMagick's format table marks AVIF as readable and writable.
- **libavif's avifenc (command line):** run `avifenc -q 75 photo.jpg photo.avif`. The avifenc tool must be built with at least one AV1 codec enabled, because none is on by default.

### Problems with JPG files

- **Banding or blocks in smooth areas**: heavy JPG compression leaves 8x8 block edges, and an AVIF made from the file keeps them. Pick the least compressed copy as the source.
- **No transparency**: a JPG cannot hold see-through pixels, so the AVIF will not have any either. Transparent pixels do not survive saving as JPEG in the first place.
- **Layers are gone**: a JPG is one flat picture, so keep the layered project file.
- **An older device rejects the file**: some older photo frames refuse progressive JPG, and saving it again without progressive mode gets around that.
- **Quality numbers disagree**: equal numbers in different editors give unequal results, so compare by eye.
- **"Image decode failed."**: the JPG could not be opened by your browser's decoder. Download the JPG again and retry.

guide.title: About JPG files
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPG file?

JPG takes its name from the Joint Photographic Experts Group, and most photographs from cameras and scanners are saved in it. The group began in 1986, and the standard is ITU-T T.81 (1992). The format is lossy: pixels are grouped in 8x8 tiles, a discrete cosine transform converts each tile, and Huffman coding packs the output.

All the major browsers show a JPG, and .jpg and .jpeg are interchangeable names, served as image/jpeg. A JPG has no transparency and cannot store layers, which matters when you place it on a colored page. A progressive JPG first draws a coarse version and sharpens it while the file loads. JPG suits web photos, camera output, mailed attachments and photo-sharing sites, and US patent protection ended in October 2006.

Editors often use a 0 to 100 scale, GIMP's default is 85, and equal numbers do not give equal quality in every program. This page has no quality setting, because the original JPG goes into the document untouched.

### Programs that open JPG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP imports a JPG for tidying a picture before it goes into a document, and ImageMagick reads JPG without a window, from the command line.
- **Web:** Google Chrome and Mozilla Firefox show a JPG when you open it in a tab.
- **Mobile:** Safari and Chrome display JPG on a phone.

### JPG and DOCX compared

- **What they are**: a JPG is one picture. A DOCX is a document, so it can hold styles, images and tables.
- **Extensions**: .jpg or .jpeg (image/jpeg) for the picture; .docx for the Word file.
- **Structure**: a DOCX is a ZIP package of XML files built on the Open Packaging Conventions. Its text and formatting are described in WordprocessingML, and images, styles and properties sit in separate parts of the package.
- **Standards**: the format is standardized twice, as ECMA-376 and as ISO/IEC 29500, and Word made it the default for new files with the 2007 release. LibreOffice Writer, ONLYOFFICE Desktop Editors, Apple Pages, Word for the web and Word for Android are listed as opening it, and some formatting attributes may differ between programs.
- **Package**: because a DOCX is a package of related parts, extracting only document.xml does not reproduce the full document.
- **Compression**: the JPG stays lossy, as it was. Placing it in a DOCX does not recompress it, because the page never decodes it first.
- **Editing**: a DOCX supports tracked changes and comments around the picture, which a bare JPG cannot hold.
- **Transparency**: a JPG has none, so the picture shows as a rectangle on the page.

The page builds the document with the docx library in your browser: one paragraph that holds the picture. The JPG's bytes are put into the package unchanged. A picture wider than 6.5 inches or taller than 9 inches is scaled down, keeping its proportions, and a smaller one keeps its size, measured at 96 pixels per inch. No text is read from the picture.

### Other ways to convert JPG to DOCX

- **Microsoft Word (Windows, Mac):** use Insert > Pictures > This Device, select the JPG, click Insert and save the file.
- **LibreOffice Writer (Windows, Mac, Linux):** choose Insert > Image, select the JPG with the Link box unmarked, then File > Save As and pick a Microsoft Word format in the File type box. LibreOffice opens and saves Word DOCX files.

### Problems with JPG files

- **A solid rectangle shows around the picture**: a JPG cannot be see-through, so it always shows as a solid rectangle. Use a format with alpha when the document needs transparency.
- **The text in the picture cannot be selected**: it is part of the image. Run OCR with the JPG to TXT converter to get the words.
- **Layers are gone**: a JPG never had any, so go back to the layered project file if you need them.
- **Blocky squares around text**: heavy compression leaves 8x8 block edges, and the DOCX carries the JPG unchanged, so start from the least compressed copy.
- **Quality numbers disagree**: a 0 to 100 setting is not a shared unit, so two editors can save the same picture at different sizes.
- **Another app changes the layout**: a different word processor can alter some formatting when it opens the DOCX.

guide.title: About JPG files
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPG file?

In JPEG, the J is for Joint, the first word of the Joint Photographic Experts Group. Its baseline mode is lossy by design: each 8x8 block of pixels gets a discrete cosine transform, and Huffman coding writes out the numbers. The group started in 1986, and its core text came out of ITU-T as T.81 in 1992; ISO and IEC took it up as 10918-1 two years after that. Cameras and scanners commonly write JPEG, and the US patents lapsed in October 2006. In progressive mode a rough picture appears first and gets sharper while more data arrives. Quality is normally a 0 to 100 slider, GIMP starts at 85, and the same figure can mean different quality in different programs.

JPEG cannot store layers, which is the main thing a designer wants to add back. The extensions .jpg and .jpeg are one and the same format, with image/jpeg as the media type. Photographs on the web, camera output, mail attachments and photo sharing all lean on it, and every major browser displays it.

### Programs that open JPG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP imports a JPG, which is handy for checking the source before you convert, and ImageMagick opens it in a terminal.
- **Web:** Chrome and Firefox display a JPG you open in a tab.
- **Mobile:** Safari and Chrome show a JPG on a phone.

### JPG and PSD compared

- **Purpose**: PSD is Adobe Photoshop's native document format. JPG is lossy and made for photographs.
- **Extensions**: .jpg or .jpeg (image/jpeg); .psd (image/vnd.adobe.photoshop).
- **Layers**: JPG stores a single flat picture. A PSD keeps layers, masks, adjustment layers and text, in sections kept apart from the image resources.
- **Compression**: JPG is lossy. PSD pixel data can be raw or encoded with RLE or ZIP compression. The PSD written here holds the decoded pixels without JPEG compression, and can be much larger than the JPG.
- **Bit depth**: JPEG channels hold 8 bits. A PSD header supports one, eight, 16 or 32 bits, though the PSD written here uses 8.
- **Size limit**: PSD tops out at 30,000 pixels for each side; PSB lifts that.
- **Signature**: a PSD header begins with 8BPS.
- **Other readers**: programs besides Photoshop must interpret Photoshop-specific data structures, so a thumbnail appearing does not prove a program can edit every part of a file.
- **Transparency**: JPG has none.

First the browser decodes the JPG. Then ImageMagick, which runs in the page, encodes those pixels as a PSD. No layers are made from the picture's contents, and EXIF, ICC profiles and XMP stay behind.

A PSD is a container with several sections. Photoshop uses those sections to hold the pieces of a design, such as layers, masks, adjustments, text and color data, so it can be edited later. The format is proprietary to Adobe, and Adobe documents its header and sections publicly.

### Other ways to convert JPG to PSD

- **Photopea (web):** choose File > Open, load the JPG, then File > Save as PSD. Photopea treats PSD as its main document format.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick picture.jpg picture.psd`. According to its format table, ImageMagick can both read and write PSD.

### Problems with JPG files

- **No layers to edit**: a JPG never stored any. The project file you exported from is the only place they can still be.
- **A blocky or smudged photo**: compression artifacts in the JPG pass straight into the PSD. Look for a less compressed copy of the picture.
- **A transparent logo shows a white box**: JPEG cannot keep see-through pixels, so the box was in the JPG before you converted it.
- **An older photo frame shows nothing**: some reject progressive JPEG, and saving the picture again without it helps.
- **Quality numbers disagree**: the same 0 to 100 value can mean different things in different editors.
- **A very large picture**: a document larger than the PSD dimension limit needs PSB or another suitable format.
- **Going back to a flat image later**: flattening a PSD into a plain image discards its structure, so keep the PSD for editing.
- **A file named .psd that will not open**: a real PSD header begins with the signature 8BPS, so a file with another header is not a PSD whatever its name says.

guide.title: About JPG files
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPG file?

A JPG stores a picture, not words. Even a photographed page of print is, inside the file, a grid of colored pixels squeezed by lossy JPEG compression, which works on 8x8 blocks of pixels. The compression comes from the Joint Photographic Experts Group, a body that started the work in 1986. ITU-T published its core standard in 1992, and ISO and IEC took it on in 1994.

Photographs on websites, in cameras, in email and on photo-sharing sites are commonly JPG, and every major browser displays it. The two names, .jpg and .jpeg, describe a single format registered as image/jpeg. The text in a photo or scan is easy to see but cannot be selected or searched, because it is only pixels. That is the gap this converter fills. A progressive JPG first shows a rough picture, then refines it as the rest arrives.

A JPG can also carry metadata such as Exif. None of that is text from the page, and none of it ends up in the TXT: only the letters the recognizer reads from the pixels do.

### Programs that open JPG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** ImageMagick reads JPG from the command line, which helps when you want to resize or straighten a batch first, and GIMP imports JPEG for editing.
- **Web:** Google Chrome and Mozilla Firefox show the picture so you can check it is legible.
- **Mobile:** Chrome and Safari show JPG on a phone.

### JPG and TXT compared

- **What they hold**: a JPG holds pixels. A TXT holds characters and nothing else.
- **Extensions**: .jpg or .jpeg (image/jpeg) against .txt (text/plain).
- **Formatting**: plain text carries no commands for typographic formatting, and it does not prescribe a page layout, a font or how images are arranged.
- **Tables and images**: a word processor can place an image or a table on a page, while plain text cannot.
- **Encoding**: a TXT depends on a character set, shown by the charset parameter. The file written here is UTF-8.
- **Editors**: Visual Studio Code and Vim open TXT on Windows, Mac and Linux, and TextEdit opens it on a Mac. Converting rich text to TXT in TextEdit removes styles and formatting.
- **Reversibility**: converting a picture to text is a reading step, not a re-save, so nothing in the TXT tells you how the page looked.

Here the recognition is done by tesseract.js, running in your browser. The worker, engine and English model are served by this site, so the picture is not sent to another site. The recognized text has line-end spaces removed and runs of three or more newlines reduced to one blank line, and it is saved as UTF-8 with a final newline. If no words are found, the page stops with an error rather than writing an empty file.

### Other ways to convert JPG to TXT

- **Tesseract (command line):** run `tesseract page.jpg result -l eng`. The command takes an input image name and an output base name, and English is the default language if -l is left out.
- **Google Drive and Docs (web):** upload the JPG to Drive, right-click it, choose Open with > Google Docs, then copy the recognized text into a plain-text editor. The image is uploaded to Google, which accepts PDF and .jpeg, .png and .gif files, asks for files of 2 MB or less, and needs the document right-side up.
- **OneNote for Mac:** insert the picture, Control-click it, choose Copy Text from Picture and paste into a text editor. Recognition uses Microsoft online services, and handwriting may not be recognized well.

### Problems with JPG files

- **Several pictures at once**: each JPG gives its own TXT, the pictures are processed in sequence, and no ZIP is made.
- **Stray blank space**: spaces at line ends are cut and three or more line breaks in a row collapse to a single blank line, so extra spacing in the picture may not carry over.
- **Other languages**: this page reads with an English model only. Use a tool with the right language data for another language.
- **"No text was found in this image."**: the page stops there instead of saving an empty file.
- **Tables lose their grid**: plain text has no table structure, so copy the result into a spreadsheet and rebuild the columns by hand.
- **Odd characters in the TXT**: an editor that reads the file with the wrong character encoding shows garbled letters. The file here is UTF-8.

guide.title: About M4V files
guide.markdown:
### What is an M4V file?

An M4V is a video file in the MPEG-4 container family. It is associated with Apple's video workflows, but the extension does not prove who made the file. Both of HandBrake's output suffixes, .m4v and .mp4, hold the same container. MP4 itself, MPEG-4 Part 14, sits on the ISO Base Media File Format, an outgrowth of Apple's QuickTime, and video files in this family carry either .mp4 or .m4v.

A container organizes timed tracks. The picture and the soundtrack are separate tracks, each with its own encoding that a player must understand, and playback depends on those encodings. The family stores timed media tracks and metadata in boxes. Turning an M4V into an MP3 makes sense when you only need the sound, because the MP3 holds no picture. The MP3 is a fresh lossy encode of the soundtrack, not a copy of the original audio.

Videos bought from the iTunes Store can carry FairPlay DRM. Use a recording you have the right to process, and keep the original M4V in case you ever need the video again.

The MP3 format, formally MPEG-1 Audio Layer III, was developed at Fraunhofer IIS from the late 1980s and became ISO/IEC 11172-3 in 1993. Being lossy, it keeps what a model of human hearing says will be noticed and drops the rest. Every major browser plays MP3, and audio/mpeg is its registered media type. That is the usual reason for this conversion: not to improve the sound, but to get a file that plays almost everywhere.

### Programs that open M4V files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** FFmpeg reads .m4v through its MOV/MP4 demuxer, and the matching decoders must be present as well. VLC media player handles MPEG-4 containers along with common MPEG-4 video and AAC audio.

### M4V and MP3 compared

- **What they hold**: an M4V holds a picture track and a soundtrack. An MP3 holds compressed sound only.
- **Compression**: MP3 is lossy; it trades some sound information for a smaller file. Re-encoding a soundtrack as MP3 is a lossy step, not a rename.
- **Metadata**: tags such as song titles live in separate ID3 structures within an MP3.
- **Bitrates**: an MP3 can be as slow as 32 kbps or as fast as 320 kbps, using a 32, 44.1 or 48 kHz sample rate.
- **Reach**: MP3 plays on nearly every device, and its patent licensing program ended in April 2017.
- **Media types**: video/mp4 and audio/mp4 for the MP4 family, audio/mpeg for MP3.

Here the picture is dropped and the soundtrack is encoded with the LAME encoder at a constant-bitrate setting that the page fixes; you cannot change it. An MP3 cannot reach that rate for audio sampled below 32 kHz, so a soundtrack sampled lower than that gets a lower bitrate. No track is chosen by you: FFmpeg's defaults pick the streams. A video without any sound cannot supply material for the encoder, so the page reports an error instead of writing an empty file. The download takes the M4V's name with an .mp3 ending, and the original video file is not changed.

The new MP3 cannot improve the original recording. Saving an edited MP3 as a new MP3 adds one more lossy pass, so keep the M4V in case you need the original sound again.

### Other ways to convert M4V to MP3

- **FFmpeg (command line):** run `ffmpeg -i input.m4v -vn -b:a 128k -c:a libmp3lame soundtrack.mp3`. The `-vn` option leaves out the picture, and The name libmp3lame refers to the LAME encoder inside FFmpeg. Decoding the input also requires the relevant decoders.

### Problems with M4V files

- **The conversion fails at once**: check that the video has an audio stream. A video with no audio track gives an error that begins "FFmpeg failed with exit code".
- **Unsupported codec**: a recognized container can still hold a codec the player lacks.
- **A new extension does not help**: renaming cannot repair damage or add support for an encoding.
- **Recording cut short**: a normal MPEG-4 family recording may be unreadable if writing ends before the required metadata is finished.
- **Very long files**: processing time depends on your device, and the page sets no length limit. Keep the M4V until you have played the downloaded MP3 to the end.

guide.title: About MP4 files
guide.markdown:
### What is an MP4 file?

Think of an MP4 as a box with compartments for picture, sound and descriptive data. Nothing in the .mp4 name reveals which codec fills each compartment, which is why a decoder must handle the compression and not merely the wrapper. H.264 video with AAC sound is the usual content, though other codecs are possible.

Every major browser can play MP4, and phones and cameras commonly produce it. Its data sits in nested boxes, and a normal file keeps its index together, which is why a recording that was interrupted before it finished can be hard to open.

Before converting, work out what the next system needs. A request that only says "Flash video" can mean H.264 and AAC, or the older Sorenson and VP6 pairings, and they are not interchangeable. If you are not sure the destination really needs FLV, ask for its list of accepted codecs first, and keep the MP4 in case the legacy copy cannot use something in it.

### Programs that open MP4 files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** ffplay plays MP4 through FFmpeg's demuxer, and mpv does desktop playback with selectable audio streams.
- **Web:** Firefox and Chrome play MP4 files whose codecs they support.
- **Mobile:** on phones, VLC for Android and for iOS opens videos saved on the device.

### MP4 and FLV compared

- **Origin**: FLV is Flash Video, a binary container tied to Macromedia's Flash video delivery. Adobe ended Flash Player support on December 31, 2020, so treat FLV as legacy media.
- **Streams**: an FLV tops out at a single video plus a single audio track, whereas an MP4 can carry many.
- **Codecs**: FLV can carry Sorenson or On2 VP6 video, and audio such as MP3, PCM or ADPCM. This page writes H.264 and AAC instead, and a player needs the decoder for whatever codecs an FLV holds.
- **Extension**: the .flv extension does not identify a unique video codec.
- **Playback**: media software such as VLC can still read FLV without Flash Player.

Picture and sound are both encoded again. The video uses H.264 (ultrafast preset, CRF 32) and the audio uses AAC at 96 kbps. Footage whose long side exceeds 1920 px is shrunk, and a frame rate above 30 per second is trimmed by discarding frames, so the running time is untouched. Sizes are rounded to even numbers too. Footage flagged interlaced is deinterlaced beforehand. This is a fresh encode, not a stream copy, so quality and file size can change.

No stream mapping is given, so FFmpeg picks the streams by its own defaults.

The download carries the MP4's name with an .flv ending, and the original file is left as it was. You can pick several MP4s; each runs in turn and becomes its own FLV, and no ZIP is made. All of it happens inside your browser, where FFmpeg runs as WebAssembly in a worker, so the video is not uploaded.

### Other ways to convert MP4 to FLV

- **FFmpeg (re-encode):** `ffmpeg -i input.mp4 -f flv -codec:v libx264 -codec:a aac output.flv` selects H.264 and AAC and names the FLV muxer with -f.
- **FFmpeg (stream copy):** `ffmpeg -i input.mp4 -c copy -f flv output.flv` skips encoding and copies the streams. An FLV has room for one video stream and one audio stream, nothing more.
- **FFmpeg (keyframe index):** `ffmpeg -i input.mp4 -codec:v libx264 -codec:a aac -flvflags add_keyframe_index output.flv` adds a keyframe index that helps seeking, particularly for HTTP pseudo streaming.

### Problems with MP4 files

- **An old player opens the container but shows no picture**: the container may be understood while the codec inside is not. Compare the player's accepted codecs with H.264 and AAC.
- **Alternate audio is missing**: an FLV keeps one audio stream, so a workflow that needs several alternative audio tracks cannot keep them in the FLV. Return to the original MP4.
- **An unfinished MP4**: an MP4 normally keeps its packet index together, so a write that was interrupted may leave a file that will not play. Cut-short input often still converts, giving a shorter result, so compare the running time.
- **Not a Flash Player file**: you do not need Flash Player for an FLV. Use any player with FLV support.
- **Keep the MP4**: making an FLV for one old workflow should not make it the only surviving copy.

The result is a movie file, not an authored DVD-Video disc.
The conversion starts from the MP4 only; the page maps no extra tracks across.

guide.title: About MP4 files
guide.markdown:
### What is an MP4 file?

In an MP4, the picture, the sound and the descriptive data each get their own track inside one container. Codecs are chosen separately from the container. The familiar pairing is H.264 picture with AAC sound, but other encodings can sit inside, so whether a file plays on older equipment depends on the streams within it as well as the wrapper.

Every major browser plays MP4, and it is a common format for phone and camera recordings and online video. Its structure is a set of nested boxes, and normal files keep their packet index together, so a recording interrupted before it is finished can be hard to play.

A request for MPG often signals a legacy playback or authoring requirement. Get the receiving system's actual specifications first: the MPEG version, picture dimensions, frame rate and supported sound. A file named .mpg does not certify that all of those have been met.

This matters most when a device manual mentions DVD. A movie file accepted by an editing program is not a finished disc, because disc authoring adds navigation and a directory structure around compliant streams. Keep the MP4 while you decide whether you need a playable file, an intermediate for authoring or a real disc.

### Programs that open MP4 files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** ffplay plays an MP4 locally, and mpv is a desktop player for the same files.
- **Web:** Chrome and Firefox can play an MP4 in a tab when they support its codecs.
- **Mobile:** you can open local files in VLC on Android or iOS.

### MP4 and MPG compared

- **Container family**: MPG is the usual extension for an MPEG program stream carrying MPEG-1 or MPEG-2 picture and sound. MP4 belongs to the MPEG-4 family. Both wrap encoded media, but they support different combinations.
- **History**: MPG was the standard extension for VCD and DVD video.
- **Suffixes**: both .mpeg and .mpg label MPEG video, and neither tells you whether the video inside is MPEG-1 or MPEG-2.
- **Streams**: some MPEG files are system streams and others are raw video, so a tool has to identify the structure before choosing a demuxer.

Here the picture is encoded as MPEG-2 and the soundtrack as MP2 at 96 kbps. Nothing from the MP4 is copied across: the video gets a new lossy pass. A long edge beyond 1920 px is scaled down, a rate above 30 frames per second is cut by dropping frames so the clip keeps its length, and widths and heights end up even. Anything flagged as interlaced gets a deinterlacing pass before encoding.

These are general conversion settings. They do not match a PAL or NTSC DVD profile, so do not treat the result as universally disc-compliant. No -map option is used; FFmpeg decides which streams go in. Your MP4 stays untouched; what you save is a new file ending in .mpg.

### Other ways to convert MP4 to MPG

- **FFmpeg (DVD target):** `ffmpeg -i input.mp4 -target ntsc-dvd output.mpg` sets the codecs, bitrates and buffer sizes for NTSC DVD. Use pal-dvd for PAL. The file still needs disc authoring if you want a navigable DVD.
- **FFmpeg (VCD target):** `ffmpeg -i input.mp4 -target pal-vcd output.mpg` applies the Video CD settings instead, for gear that expects them.

### Problems with MP4 files

- **A player rejects the MPG**: compare its streams with the device manual. The extension does not settle bitrate, dimensions, scan type or accepted audio. A standard-definition MPEG device may refuse a larger MPEG-2 file that a desktop player handles.
- **It won't act as a DVD**: burning one MPG as data is not the same as building a DVD-Video layout with navigation and supporting files.
- **Lost detail**: a lossy MPEG encode cannot keep every detail of the picture, and a large frame may also be resized.
- **Decoder missing**: playback needs a decoder for the sound as well as the picture, and sharing a container does not make their codecs interchangeable.
- **Unfinished MP4**: a recording stopped mid-write may be unplayable. The output from a cut-short input can end early, so check its length.

For an equipment handoff, ask for a short sample known to play on that device and compare its specifications with your export. That beats matching a suffix.

faqs.question: How do I convert MPV to MP4?
faqs.answer: Add the .mpv file above and give the page a moment. It turns the picture into H.264 inside your browser and hands back an MP4 to download. Nothing is uploaded.

faqs.question: Why is my MP4 silent?
faqs.answer: A true MPV is a video elementary stream, so it has no soundtrack inside it. The conversion cannot create sound; the audio, if there is any, sits in a separate file.

faqs.question: Is .mpv the same as the mpv media player?
faqs.answer: No. One is a filename extension for MPEG video; the other is a media-player application that opens many formats. Playing a movie in mpv does not make it an MPV file.

faqs.question: Does the page copy the MPEG video into the MP4 unchanged?
faqs.answer: No. It re-encodes the picture as H.264, so the MP4 is a new lossy copy.

faqs.question: Can I add the matching audio file here?
faqs.answer: No. The page converts the one file you pick. To join a separate audio file with the picture, use a desktop tool such as FFmpeg that accepts two inputs.

faqs.question: How large can the MP4 picture be?
faqs.answer: The longest edge tops out at 1920 px, with bigger frames scaled down. Both sides also end up even, which can take a pixel off an odd-sized frame.

faqs.question: Is the source frame rate kept?
faqs.answer: Rates above 30 fps are held at 30. Anything slower stays as it was.

faqs.question: Does the page deinterlace?
faqs.answer: Yes, for frames flagged as interlaced; they are deinterlaced before encoding. Progressive material is not changed by that step.

faqs.question: Can I rename my .mpv file to .mp4?
faqs.answer: No. Renaming does not build the MP4 track and timing structure, and Adobe warns that a changed extension does not guarantee import. A real conversion writes the container.

faqs.question: Should I keep the original MPV and its audio?
faqs.answer: Yes. Keep the MPV and any matching audio file until you have watched the finished MP4 to the end.

guide.title: About MPV files
guide.markdown:
### What is an MPV file?

An MPV is usually an MPEG video elementary stream. It holds the encoded picture sequence itself, not a program container that interleaves picture and sound. FFmpeg's raw MPEG demuxer recognizes such video sequences from their contents, and it tells them apart from MPEG packets that contain audio. Adobe groups the .mpv suffix with MPEG-1 imports.

A companion audio file may sit beside the MPV, but the video bytes do not contain that sound. In short, the extension stands for an MPEG video elementary stream, typically MPEG-1 or MPEG-2 video without audio. That is why a player that opens whole movies can find nothing familiar in it, and why the sound has to be handled as a separate job.

The name is easy to confuse with mpv, the media-player application. The two are unrelated: watching a movie in the player does not make it an MPV elementary stream. Inspect the actual file before deciding how to convert it, because the extension alone should not decide whether MPEG-1 or MPEG-2 decoding is needed.

### Programs that open MPV files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** FFmpeg, whose raw MPEG demuxer recognizes video sequences from their contents, and ffplay, which plays them through the FFmpeg libraries when MPEG decoding is included.
- **Windows and Mac:** Adobe After Effects lists .mpv among its MPEG-1 import extensions.

### MPV and MP4 compared

- **Streams**: a genuine MPV supplies picture only. An MP4 stores timed tracks, so it can hold video and audio together.
- **Wrapper**: a raw MPEG video stream has no program-stream wrapper. The MP4 adds the track and timing structure.
- **Compatibility**: Premiere Elements lists MPV among its unsupported extensions, while Adobe Media Encoder lists it among recognized MPEG input extensions.
- **Codecs**: the .mp4 name does not name a codec, and every major browser plays MP4.

Here the picture is encoded again as H.264 with FFmpeg's ultrafast preset at CRF 32, and the MP4 is written with its index at the start of the file so it can begin playing before the download finishes. Audio is set to AAC at 96 kbps, but an MPV that carries none leaves the MP4 silent. Output cannot exceed 1920 px along its longest edge or 30 frames per second, each side is made even, and frames flagged as interlaced are deinterlaced. Smaller or slower footage stays below those limits.

Files you add are processed in turn, and each produces a separate MP4; there is no ZIP. The encoder is FFmpeg built for WebAssembly and it runs in the page, so nothing is uploaded. The download takes the MPV's name with an .mp4 ending, leaving your MPV unaltered.

An MP4 is built from nested boxes that describe each track and its timing. H.264 with AAC is the pairing most files use, though the container also carries other codecs, so the .mp4 name alone does not tell a player what is inside.

For an MPV, the practical gain is the container itself. The picture gets a track, a timeline and a place to put sound later, which a bare elementary stream does not offer. Adobe Media Encoder and After Effects both recognize the suffix, so the MPV can still be imported there if that is the real goal.

### Other ways to convert MPV to MP4

- **FFmpeg (H.264 re-encode):** `ffmpeg -i input.mpv -an -pix_fmt yuv420p -c:v libx264 output.mp4` makes a video-only H.264 copy.
- **FFmpeg (stream copy):** `ffmpeg -i input.mpv -c:v copy -an output.mp4` puts the MPEG video into an MP4 without re-encoding, so the MP4 still holds MPEG video.
- **FFmpeg (fast start):** `ffmpeg -i input.mpv -an -movflags +faststart -c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p output.mp4` moves the index to the start of the file in a second pass, which suits web playback.

### Problems with MPV files

- **The MP4 is silent**: an elementary video stream has no soundtrack inside its video data. Find the matching audio file and join the two with a desktop tool; converting the picture again will not add sound.
- **A movie player won't open it**: the stream has no container around it, so a player that expects one may not open it.
- **Adobe won't import it**: Premiere Elements lists MPV as unsupported, and renaming the extension does not help. Convert first.
- **Unclear MPEG version**: inspect the stream to see which kind of MPEG video it holds.
